#### About Karl Popper

Karl Popper (1902–1994) was an Austrian-born philosopher of science and politics who spent his mature career in New Zealand and at the London School of Economics. Fleeing Nazism, he developed critical rationalism against verificationism and historicist prophecy.

### Interpretation

Popper is contrasting two postures toward history. The prophet claims to know where history is going and therefore treats people as material for a predicted outcome; the maker accepts uncertainty and acts within it, remaining corrigible. His claim is that the first posture produces worse results as well as worse politics, because it removes the possibility of learning from error. The sentence is the conclusion of his argument against historicism.

#### Why it matters

The distinction is practical: predicting removes your ability to be wrong, and anything that removes that also removes your ability to correct course.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “We may become the makers of our fate…”?

“We may become the makers of our fate…” comes from The Open Society and Its Enemies, attributed to Karl Popper.

#### What does Karl Popper mean by fate?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Epictetus and Seneca), fate is framed through Stoicism and Philosophy of Will. Some passages define fate; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through fate, critique, freedom.
